prompt: Review the following design requirements for a local inference engine. Explain the trade-offs after reading all requirements. The engine runs on a workstation with a CPU, ordinary host memory, and a discrete GPU connected through PCIe. All required model experts must execute and their original router probabilities must be preserved. The objective is lower total request latency without silently reducing answer quality. Requirement A: During prompt processing, group token rows by expert so repeated expert use can amortize weight transfers. Count the actual routed rows rather than assuming a uniform distribution. Preserve their ordering when merging outputs. Requirement B: During generation, do not upload expert weights unless the expected reduction in CPU work exceeds transfer and synchronization costs. Account for eviction of useful GPU residents and competing host memory traffic. Requirement C: Use bounded staging buffers and wait for pending reads before recycling them. Pinned memory is a scarce resource, not an unlimited substitute for GPU memory. Requirement D: Compare candidates against the unchanged native engine and the current hybrid path with identical prompts, sampling, context capacity, thread counts, and output limits. Report prompt throughput separately from generation throughput and total wall time. Requirement E: Tests must cover per-token routing, strided tensors, several expert counts, partial CPU/GPU splits, and empty work on either device. Do not renormalize the router probabilities separately for the two branches. Requirement F: Measure cache admission and migration costs rather than selecting a policy solely from cache hit rate. A larger hit rate can still lose because of bandwidth consumption, cache pollution, or synchronization. Requirement G: A timing sample with missing computation, invalid dimensions, failed transfers, or numerical errors cannot be counted as an acceleration result. Preserve failed attempts in the experiment ledger. Requirement H: Use independent scalar tests for small synthetic cases and aligned full-vocabulary comparisons for the real target graph. Successful output formatting is not evidence of broad answer quality. Requirement I: Resident weight execution and execution that includes uploading those weights are distinct experiments. Make their timing boundaries explicit, especially whether source preparation, output staging, and final synchronization are included. Requirement J: The same scheduling policy need not be optimal for short prompts, long prompts, and single-token generation. First measure the relevant work distributions and hardware costs, then test a stage-aware decision rule. Requirement K: A proof of concept must not modify application defaults, reset shared hardware, or interrupt an active user request. Research processes must release GPU allocations before application validation. Requirement L: Report improvements only for measured conditions and preserve the previous working path as a control. Do not infer full-model token rates by multiplying an isolated layer time by the number of layers. Summarize which requirements protect correctness, which protect resource bounds, and which are necessary for reliable performance comparisons.

Analyze this independent deployment checklist and propose a measurement sequence. A local service uses a discrete GPU as a fast working set for experts that otherwise reside in system RAM. The CPU can execute cold experts in place, exchanging activation-scale values rather than whole parameter tensors. The service must retain original weights and must execute every expert selected by the model. Checklist item one concerns workload accounting: distinguish prompt processing from autoregressive generation, distinguish accepted output tokens from verification positions, and distinguish one conversation's latency from aggregate throughput. Checklist item two concerns routing: record how many token rows use each expert in each layer and each evaluation microbatch. Do not assume equal popularity or identical expert choices across token rows. The final layer may be pruned to output positions, so an observer must report its actual coverage rather than presenting a partial graph as a complete prompt trace. Checklist item three concerns transfers: measure bytes, staging copies, host memory reads, synchronization, and destination availability. Treat pageable synchronous uploads and pinned asynchronous uploads as separate mechanisms. Account for pending consumers when reusing a staging allocation. Checklist item four concerns CPU execution: compare thread counts under the actual layer workload, preserve the native quantization semantics, and measure contention with concurrent DMA. A faster kernel with a different approximation is not automatically equivalent to the original execution path. Checklist item five concerns GPU execution: inspect operation support, tensor dimensions, precision requirements, and view ownership. A view must retain the backend and storage of its source, and a copied tensor must have the expected shape and strides. Compare resident execution separately from transient execution. Checklist item six concerns admission: protect current selections, charge evicted residents' lost benefit, and measure whether new residency survives long enough to repay its upload. Training-only frequency data must not include held-out future requests. Checklist item seven concerns correctness: validate the earliest divergent intermediate rather than loosening a final-logit tolerance. Repeat controls to distinguish native placement variation from candidate-specific errors. A candidate must not replace required failed work with a zero vector and continue as though the sample succeeded. Checklist item eight concerns reporting: keep original command failures, failed numerical gates, and unfavorable workload results. Record source revisions and timing boundaries. Use repeated matched controls and alternate experiment order. Avoid selecting the fastest single noisy run. Checklist item nine concerns resources: preserve per-request context capacity when comparing different policies, count expert banks and temporary buffers together, and ensure GPU contexts are released before restoring other workloads. Do not assume a limited number of CPU cores reproduces a different machine's memory channels or capacity. Checklist item ten concerns stage-aware scheduling: an expert with many prompt rows may justify a GPU upload even when uploading it for one generated token would lose. Measure the crossover instead of using a universal threshold from another model or machine. Cache state after prefill may also change subsequent decode behavior, so the final decision must consider whole-request time rather than prefill speed alone. Checklist item eleven concerns observations: synchronization introduced by tensor capture can change scheduling and fusion. Instrumented routing traces can describe work distributions but cannot establish uninstrumented serving speed. Check whether disabling the observer changes sampled output. Checklist item twelve concerns deployment: research findings belong in a separate experiment first. Application changes require their own correctness and performance qualification, and a known working standard path must remain available. Explain how you would order these measurements to avoid premature optimization and misleading speedup claims.
